'''''Euphorbia cotinifolia''''' is a broadleaf red shrub native to Mexico and South America. The scientific name of the plant comes from the words ''cotinus'' meaning "smoketree" and ''folia'' meaning "leaf".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/plant-finder/plant-details/kc/d824/euphorbia-cotinifolia.aspx|title=Euphorbia cotinifolia|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden|access-date=30 December 2012}}</ref>  Common names for the species include '''smoketree spurge''', '''tropical smoke bush''', '''Caribbean copper plant''',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.finegardening.com/plantguide/euphorbia-cotinifolia-tropical-smoke-bush.aspx|title=Euphorbia cotinifolia (Tropical smoke bush, Caribbean copper plant) - Fine Gardening Plant Guide|access-date=30 December 2012}}</ref> and '''Mexican shrubby spurge'''.<ref name=USDA>{{PLANTS|symbol=EUCO24|taxon=Euphorbia cotinifolia|accessdate=26 April 2015}}</ref>

==Description==
Treated as a shrub, it is a [[semi-deciduous]] shrub reaches {{convert|10|to|15|ft|m|abbr=on}} but can be grown as a tree reaching {{convert|30|ft|m|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Jacaranda mimosifolia |url=https://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=616 |website=San Marcos Growers |access-date=20 July 2026}}</ref> Small white flowers with creamy bracts bloom at the ends of the branches in summer. The purplish stems, when broken, exude a sap that is a skin irritant.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Nelson|first1=Lewis S.|last2=Shih|first2=Richard D.|last3=Balick|first3=Michael J.|isbn=978-0-387-33817-0|title=Handbook of Poisonous and Injurious Plants|edition=2nd|year=2007|publisher=Springer|page=162}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
The species is well known in Central America, where its poisonous sap has been used both as a medicine and a poison.  As a medicine, it has been used in [[folk remedies]] as both an [[emetic]] and [[cathartic]] substance.  Fishermen have been known to add the sap to water in fishing grounds to stun fish and force them to float to the top.  It was also historically used as a poison for arrowheads by the natives of [[Curaçao]].<ref name="clay">{{cite book|last1=Clay|first1=Horace F.|last2=Hubbard|first2=James C. |last3=Golt |first3=Rick |title=Tropical Shrubs Paper |year=1987 |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |isbn=978-0-8248-1128-0 |page=72}}</ref>

The sap can cause irritation if it comes into contact with human skin or eyes.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nelson |first1=Lewis S. |last2=Shih |first2=Richard D. |last3=Balick |first3=Michael J. |isbn=978-0-387-33817-0|title=Handbook of Poisonous and Injurious Plants |edition=2nd |year=2007 |publisher=Springer |page=162}}</ref>  If ingested, the sap can cause severe damage to [[internal organs]].<ref name="clay" />

==Gardening==
''Euphorbia cotinifolia'' is commonly grown as an ornamental plant in gardens and in pots, due to its colourful and distinctive foliage.  It prefers a site with well-drained soil and full sun.  While relatively hardy, it does not react well to wind, salt, or frost.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Weissich, Paul R. |author2=Rauch, Fred D. |title=Plants for tropical landscapes: a gardener's guide |publisher=University of Hawai'i Press |location=Honolulu |year=2000 |pages=50 |isbn=978-0-8248-2034-3}}</ref>
